claim_grading_standard.DISPUTED: Credible sources disagree; brief must present both sides.
claim_grading_standard.PROVISIONAL: Single-source or indirect evidence; usable with explicit caveat.
claim_grading_standard.SUPPORTED: Corroborated by credible scholarship, institutional records, or multiple independent sources.
claim_grading_standard.UNRESOLVED: Claim asserted in task or search context but no adequate source located; recorded so the gap is visible.
claim_grading_standard.VERIFIED: Directly confirmed by a primary or institutional source inspected in this research pass.

claims.claim: The Great Migration stimulated new urban religious practices in Black Chicago that combined southern traditions with the conditions of northern city life.
claims.evidence: Princeton University Press introduction to Best, 'Passionately Human, No Less Divine' (2005): migration 'stimulated urban religious practices combining southern traditions with urban conditions.'
claims.notes: Scholarly interpretation from a peer-reviewed monograph introduction; full text not inspected in this pass.

claims.claim: Many Black Chicago churches in the migration era had memberships more than 70% women.
claims.evidence: Best (2005) introduction, as indexed via Princeton University Press chapter PDF.
claims.notes: Quantitative assertion inside scholarly work; original underlying survey data not inspected here.

claims.claim: Class and regional conflict between migrants and established residents altered mainstream Black Chicago worship: church music, emotional expression, and social-service programs all changed.
claims.evidence: Best (2005) introduction.
claims.notes: Interpretive claim; corroborated in its music dimension by the Dorsey/gospel institutional record (C15).

claims.claim: Gospel became prominent in Black Chicago when mainstream churches responded to southern migrants' demands for the worship styles they knew.
claims.evidence: Best (2005) introduction; institutional corroboration via Pilgrim Baptist music history (C15) and Morning Star gospel services (C09).
claims.notes: Mechanism (demand-driven adoption) is Best's argument; the institutional outcomes are independently documented.

claims.claim: Black churches, especially poor and working-class congregations, served as proving grounds for gospel singers.
claims.evidence: Best (2005) introduction; corroborated by Morning Star/Barrett Sisters case (C10).

claims.claim: Morning Star Baptist Church of Chicago was founded in 1917 by 25 members, many of them Great Migration arrivals.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago, 'Morning Star Baptist Church of Chicago Final Landmark Recommendation,' adopted April 3, 2025.
claims.notes: Municipal landmark designation report; a formal institutional document with cited research.

claims.claim: Morning Star materially supported the Chicago Urban League with money, sleeping accommodations, and meals, and served 2,514 meals to unemployed people and families in April 1921.
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025), citing congregational and Urban League records.
claims.notes: Quantitative figure from institutional history; underlying primary records not directly inspected.

claims.claim: Morning Star's building hosted non-worship activity including UNIA lectures, films, and the Black Cross Nurses.
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025).
claims.notes: Demonstrates the church building as a multi-use civic space, not a Sunday-only sanctuary.

claims.claim: At Morning Star, gospel services, concerts, and related events functioned as both religious and social gatherings.
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025).
claims.notes: Supports the intersection thesis directly: music events were social infrastructure.

claims.claim: The Barrett Sisters were nurtured in the Morning Star choir starting as children in the 1930s, and talent circulated between Morning Star and Pilgrim Baptist.
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025).
claims.notes: Institutional case for cross-congregational music training networks feeding Sunday musical life.

claims.claim: Morning Star's original garage conversion included a second-floor kitchen, and the 1937-1939 conversion of an auto garage into a church involved congregational tradesmen (per building permits and recollection).
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025), citing building permit records and congregational recollection.
claims.notes: Material-infrastructure claim: the kitchen is the built evidence for fellowship/service meals inside the church.

claims.claim: In 1993-2003 Morning Star added a newsletter, tape ministry, Kitchen Chat, and drama ministry, showing late-century adaptation of programs and media.
claims.evidence: Morning Star landmark report (2025).
claims.notes: Generational-change evidence: tape ministry marks the recorded-media era of Sunday life.

claims.claim: In the 1930s, six Black maids at Chicago's Roosevelt Hotel rejected a rotating arrangement giving only some workers occasional free Sundays, demanded all Sundays off, and walked out after the demand was refused; Sunday was described as reserved for religious/community work and rest.
claims.evidence: Ervin (2015) article, as quoted in search-indexed snippet; full text and complete bibliographic metadata NOT verified in this pass.
claims.notes: Key counterpoint evidence. Use with explicit caveat. Full citation must be resolved before any VERIFIED/SUPPORTED upgrade. Do not build arguments that collapse if this episode is misattributed.

claims.claim: Black women's domestic and service work structurally conflicted with Sunday worship participation; domestic workers were excluded from the 1935 National Labor Relations Act's protections, leaving Sunday-off demands without legal backing.
claims.evidence: In These Times (2011), 'Struggle Hasn't Changed for The Help of Today': notes NLRA (1935) exclusion of domestic workers and documents Chicago domestic workers' conditions; historical framing corroborated by Jones, 'Labor of Love, Labor of Sorrow' (1985), not fully consulted.
claims.notes: The NLRA exclusion is a well-established legal fact; the article is journalistic rather than scholarly. Scope: national law, Chicago application.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey was music director at Pilgrim Baptist Church from 1932 into the late 1970s, established a Black gospel publishing firm, and co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses in 1932.
claims.evidence: Religion News Service (2006), on the loss of historic Pilgrim Baptist Church.
claims.notes: Journalistic report from a religion-news wire; institutional music-system claim, not a celebrity profile.

claims.claim: Pilgrim Baptist's lost archive reportedly included announcements, concert and program notes, and Sunday school attendance records dating to 1922.
claims.evidence: Religion News Service (2006).
claims.notes: 'Reportedly' preserved from source; archive destroyed in the 2006 Pilgrim fire. Establishes the documentary genres Sunday produced.

claims.claim: An urban Black Holiness church Sunday service (ethnography, 1978) featured choir-led 'getting happy,' differentiated congregational participation, an altar call, a collection, and the concept of a 'church home.'
claims.evidence: Burns & Smith, 'The Symbolism of Becoming in the Sunday Service of an Urban Black Holiness Church,' Anthropological Quarterly 51(3), 1978, pp. 185-204, via search-accessible text.
claims.notes: Peer-reviewed ethnography, but its city was NOT verified as Chicago in this pass. Use only as comparative context, explicitly labeled.

claims.claim: Chicago's Black population share rose from 2% (1910) to 7% (1930), 8% (1940), 14% (1950), 23% (1960), and 38% (1975); the African American population grew from about 278,000 in 1940 to about 813,000 in 1960.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago (population percentages); Chicago Urban League 'CULtivate Part 1' report (population totals). The 1940 figures are mutually consistent (8% of ~3.4M ≈ 272,000).
claims.notes: Standard demographic context; no contradiction found between the two sources.

claims.claim: In Black church culture, 'Sunday best' dress functioned as dignity and respectability assertion against racist stereotypes, and was simultaneously subject to gendered policing and class exclusion.
claims.evidence: Ford, 'SNCC Women, Denim, and the Politics of Dress' (scholarship on dress politics); Northeastern writing article on dress and respectability; RNS (2004) on generational shifts in church dress.
claims.notes: SCOPE LIMIT: the dress-politics scholarship is not Chicago-specific. RNS 2004 is outside the brief's period and usable only as retrospective evidence of late-century change.

claims.claim: No Chicago-specific evidence was located in this pass establishing which garments Black Chicagoans could afford for Sunday, or how affordability stratified Sunday dress locally.
claims.evidence: Negative search result: located dress scholarship is national/Southern; located Chicago sources do not address garment affordability.
claims.notes: Major gap. The brief must not universalize 'Sunday best' claims to Chicago without this evidence.

claims.claim: One Chicago family account ('Uncle Don,' Mississippi roots, Chicago-born) describes Sunday gatherings with potato salad, collard greens, fried chicken, grace before the meal, and a large table, and frames the practice as carried from Mississippi to Chicago across generations.
claims.evidence: The African American Folklorist, 'Black Southern Food Tradition' oral-history-style interview.
claims.notes: ONE family case, single web source of uncertain editorial rigor. Illustrates, never proves, citywide menu claims. Fixed-menu generalizations are excluded by this grade.

claims.claim: A common Baptist Sunday sequence ran Sunday School, morning worship, Baptist Training Union, and evening worship, with BTU training age groups in doctrine, public speaking, fellowship, and leadership.
claims.evidence: General Baptist records (Watauga history; West, 'Beyond the Stained Glass'), NOT from Chicago Black congregations.
claims.notes: Comparative model only. Chicago Black congregational verification requires church programs or Defender church-page evidence not located in this pass.

claims.claim: Church anniversary programs commonly preserve institutional histories, member photographs, organizational histories, and local advertisements (Jones Memorial Baptist Church 1946 program, Philadelphia, 36 pages); Miles Mark Fisher's 'History of the Olivet Baptist Church of Chicago' cites a 'Souvenir Program Olivet Baptist Church, 1915.'
claims.evidence: AbeBooks listing for Jones Memorial program (genre evidence); Internet Archive full text of Fisher's Olivet history (Chicago existence evidence).
claims.notes: Genre claim is comparative (Philadelphia example); the Olivet 1915 program's existence is cited within a scholarly Chicago church history. No Chicago anniversary program was directly inspected.

claims.claim: The South Side Home Movie Project (UChicago, founded 2005 by Jacqueline Stewart) preserves 200+ home movies (1929-1982), later 1,200+ reels (1930s-1980s), of South Side family and community life: birthdays, holidays, picnics, parades, eating, dancing, travel.
claims.evidence: UChicago News; UChicago Civic Engagement (2025 exhibition).
claims.notes: Institutional archive of ordinary Black Chicago family life. Sunday-specific content was NOT verified in any reel; do not claim Sunday coverage.

claims.claim: 'Dinner' is used here for the main Sunday meal, often served midday or early afternoon in southern and Midwestern Black usage; 'supper' for a later or lighter evening meal where sources use the term. Usage varies by family.
claims.evidence: Popular/terminology sources only; no Chicago-specific linguistic documentation located.
claims.notes: Operational definition for the brief's consistency, not a verified Chicago speech-pattern claim.

claims.claim: 'Say Amen, Somebody' (1982, dir. George T. Nierenberg; 4K restoration supported by NMAAHC) documents Thomas A. Dorsey, Mother Willie Mae Ford Smith, and the Barrett Sisters — central figures of the Chicago gospel tradition that fed Sunday musical life.
claims.evidence: Film at Lincoln Center program description; Kino Lorber release notes; NMAAHC 'Through the African American Lens' program page.
claims.notes: The film illustrates the music system; it is not evidence for any specific Sunday routine claim.

claims.claim: V01 photograph: 'Pastor of the Pentecostal Church, Chicago, Illinois,' by Russell Lee; NYPL Digital Collections Image ID 1260227; Schomburg Center, Photographs and Prints Division; NYPL date range 1935-1944; NYPL believes the item is public domain in the United States; subject described as an African American woman pastor seated, listening to a church choir.
claims.date_range: 1935-1944 (NYPL date range; likely April 1941 FSA Chicago work — do not assert the narrower date without item-level confirmation)
claims.evidence: NYPL Digital Collections item page, inspected September 28, 2026; IIIF download performed same date.
claims.notes: Artifact-level facts only. Do not infer the congregation's denomination beyond NYPL's title, or the service's day beyond the research context.
